projectDesc.p: The digital part of the SNSF project 'Caroline Spurgeon: Chaucer Allusions, Shakespeare's Imagery, and the Digital Humanities' aims to create the first open-access database dedicated to the criticism and reception of Chaucer throughout history. It draws on the compilation and cataloguing work carried out by Professor Caroline Spurgeon (1869–1942) and collected in 'Five Hundred Years of Chaucer Criticism and Allusion'. This work consists of three volumes and a supplement, which will be systematically transcribed, corrected, enriched, encoded and published online, in order to facilitate future research and bring new perspectives to light.

editorialDecl.p: The original spelling and punctuation are retained. Meaningful layouts are reproduced, i.e. verses, printed marginalia, dots lines, tables, etc. However, we do not consider, the line breaks for prose, the columns or the curly brackets. The same rules apply for special characters and glyphs. Otiose letters are normalised, as well as spaces before punctuation marks.

ab.seg: [p. 269] [Mr. Mather describes the Compotus referring to Chaucer's first Italian journey in Roll of Foreign Accts., fixes the duration of Chaucer's absence, and argues for the commence- ment of the 'Italian Period' in 1379, after the second Italian journey. For the text of the Compotus and further notes see Mod. Lang. Notes, 1896, vol. xi, pp. 210-13, 255-6; 1897, vol. xii, 9-10. See also under Mather, 1896, above.] [pp. 309- [Miss M. A. Scott urges the date of the first Italian journey 10] for the commencement of the Italian period, and holding it 'a natural inference' that Chaucer then met Petrarch, she lays stress on Petrarch's attraction for Chaucer on the score of style. [p. 365] [Dr. Flügel calls attention to the fact that he had himself deduced from dates printed in Dr. Furnivall's Fresh Chaucer Notices, 1873 (p. 130), the duration of Chaucer's first Italian journey, and had published his conclusions in a review of Skeat's Chaucer (Dial, Feb. 16, 1895). [Mr. Hinckley opposes Miss Scott's tacit 'assumption that Chaucer is to be identified with the "Clerk of Oxenford,'" and dismisses his identification with the Squire. [p. 385] [Mr. Mather replies to Dr. Flügel, adding a note on Dr. Furnivall’s statement of the dates.]
